anchors.fact: On the night of 6 January 1909, at 88° 7′ S, Shackleton admitted it must be the last outward march with the sledge, saying nature and too little food had beaten them. Two days in the tent in a blizzard followed. On 9 January they left the sledge and pushed on to 88° 23′ S, about 180 km from the Pole (SPRI: "within 180km"; our sum is 179.6 km). They raised the flag, turned their backs on the Pole, and he wrote that failure was theirs, though they had done their best to avoid it. (F7–F10, S1)
anchors.meaning: He called it failure; the Scott Polar Research Institute calls it "the brave decision to turn for home". The guest files their own turn-rounds the same way.

anchors.fact: At New Year 1909 (the passage isn't pinned to the day), he wrote that he made himself consider the lives of the men with him, and that going too far would make getting back impossible. He kept going south for days afterwards. (F3, F5, F23)
anchors.meaning: Only "he made himself consider". "He turned back for them" and "one sum since New Year" are the bartender's **I like to think**.

anchors.fact: Same passage: the science was done, "But all this was not the Pole. And how sadly I realised that I need not say." (F4)
anchors.meaning: The want he swallowed, on his own page.

anchors.fact: Two days in the bags in "shrieking blizzard", the food going without marching, fearing the tracks to the depot would drift over. (F8)
anchors.meaning: Stuck, with other people's lives on your count.

anchors.fact: The Bluff depot was "the one which I had told Joyce to lay out" (Ernest Joyce, in charge of dogs and sledges), "the one ray of hope". Without it they hadn't food enough to reach the ship. Joyce stocked it in two journeys, and it held luxuries in plenty and an ample supply. (F11, F21, 526)
anchors.meaning: The sum only worked because he'd laid down the way home before he left.

anchors.fact: Marshall's illness grew worse. Shackleton left him in Adams's care and pushed on with Wild, found the hut empty, and reached the ship on 1 March: "the load which was suddenly lifted from my shoulders". That same afternoon he set out again to bring in Adams and Marshall. On 4 March the entire expedition was safe on board (date only: the book gives 1 a.m. and 2 a.m.). Dossier only: Adams nearly went over the ice edge within sight of the ship. (F12–F18, F22)
anchors.meaning: Everyone home is the only summit that counts, and he went back out for it the day he could have rested. Never "no man left behind".

anchors.fact: Joyce's party left Carlsbad plums at the depot: a preserved plum sweet, sold boxed as a luxury (1891 London cookbook, 1900 German exhibit, 1952 analyst). Never "candied" or "stuffed". (P1–P5)
anchors.meaning: Our fresh-plum syrup is a stand-in, owned in one clause: a nod to what was waiting and the planning behind it. Never "the plums they found".

anchors.fact: Antarctic Heritage Trust conservators found crates of Mackinlay's in the ice under his 1908 hut at Cape Royds (no find year). Whyte & Mackay, which owns the brand, recreated the whisky as a limited edition, then (April 2017) launched Shackleton, a blended malt "inspired by" him and using the recreation as its "foundation". (W1, W4, W5, W8, W10)
anchors.meaning: The link, never the mirror. Say "a blended malt named for him and built on a recreation of the whisky his expedition left under its hut", never the hut whisky, never "his whisky".

anchors.fact: Plum is on the *Flavor Matrix*'s Grain wheel (pdf 137, rendered), not in Grain's listed pairings (pdf 136). The syrup is adapted from the *Codex*'s Blended Strawberry Syrup (p. 47). (card)
The famous ship: *Endurance* was trapped in the pack ice and "finally crushed by the pressure" (SPRI). (S2)
anchors.meaning: One clause in y1, to set it aside. Never in the image.

cocktail.closingLine: Drink to the top you turned round from. It was still the right place to turn.
cocktail.glassware: a heavy double tumbler, one large clear cube
method: **The plum syrup (about 20 minutes; makes about 220 ml, enough for about 35 drinks).** Stone 100 g of ripe plums and throw the stones away whole; don't crack them. Blend the flesh, skins and all, until smooth. Put it in a small pan with 200 g of white sugar and warm it gently, stirring, just until the sugar has dissolved; don't let it boil. Press it through a fine sieve and let it cool. It keeps in the fridge for about a week; if it ever tastes fizzy, throw it out.
Put the plum syrup and the bitters in the tumbler, then the whisky, and stir to mix.
Add one large ice cube and stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels cold.
Twist the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Far Enough

recipe.item: Shackleton blended malt Scotch whisky (40%), recommended, or any Highland blended malt Scotch, 40-43%
recipe.note: a blended malt named for him and built on a recreation of the whisky his expedition left under its hut

recipe.item: rich plum syrup, made at home from ripe plums
recipe.note: a nod to the preserved plums waiting at the last depot on the way back; fresh plums stand in for them

cocktail.tagline: You'll take them anywhere. You'll bring every one of them back.

reading.epigraph: They turned round 180 km from the South Pole. This glass is for the way home.
whoYouAre: It was your idea in the first place: the hill, the all-day walk, the trip nobody else would have booked. Then, a couple of hundred metres below the top, the cloud comes down, someone has gone quiet, and you hear yourself say it: "Right. Turning round." The groan. The long way down. In the car park you count heads, and nobody notices you're counting.

You'll go as far as everyone can get back from, and not a step further. You wanted that top more than any of them. You swallow it on the spot, so nobody has to feel they cost you anything, and later, privately, you file the day under "didn't make it". The fear is getting stranded somewhere you led people, with no plan that gets every one of them home. And that's what your turning round gives the people with you: they go further in your company than they'd dare alone, because they know you'll turn round in time. You earn that trust every time you turn.
yours: You may know the story of Ernest Shackleton's ship, crushed in the ice. Years before it, he walked towards the South Pole with three others, Frank Wild, Eric Marshall and Jameson Adams, hauling sledges onto the high plateau. At New Year 1909, short of food, he wrote that he made himself "consider the lives of those who were with me": go on too far, and they could never get back. He kept going south for days afterwards. On 6 January he admitted, that night, that it had to be their last march south with the sledge. Then a blizzard pinned them in their tent for two days, with the food going. On 9 January they left the sledge, pushed on to about 180 km from the Pole, planted the flag, turned their backs on the Pole, and started home. He wrote that failure was theirs, though they had done their best to avoid it. The Scott Polar Research Institute calls it "the brave decision to turn for home".

The way home was hunger and storms, from one store of food to the next. He had told one of his men, Ernest Joyce, to lay out the last big store, and he called it the one ray of hope in front of them. When they reached it there were plums and plum puddings waiting. Then Marshall's illness grew worse. Shackleton left him with Adams and pushed on with Wild to catch the ship, and found the hut empty. When they finally got aboard, he wrote of the load suddenly lifted from his shoulders. That same afternoon he set off again, to bring in the other two. On 4 March the whole expedition was safe on board.

I like to think Shackleton had been doing one sum since New Year: how far four people could go and still all get back. He gave the weather and the food as his reason, and both were real. But I think the food was the road home, and he turned while it could still get them all back, with that last store counted in. That's you. You go as far as everyone can get back from, you hold your own wanting until the last possible moment, and then you turn. "But all this was not the Pole," he wrote. "And how sadly I realised that I need not say." You know that sentence. You've just never said it out loud.

The cocktail I've made for you is a whisky Old-Fashioned, as great a classic as there is. That classic is built from things that keep: whisky, sugar, bitters and water. I've added one that doesn't. The plums at Shackleton's depot were preserved ones, a boxed luxury; mine are fresh and blended into a rich syrup: a nod to what was waiting at that last store, and to the planning that put it there. I'd pour Shackleton, a blended malt named for him and built on a recreation of the whisky his expedition left under its hut in Antarctica, or any Highland blended malt Scotch. It's built over one big cube in a heavy tumbler, the kind of glass that stands steady wherever you set it down, and orange peel finishes it.

So stop keeping that file. Every turn-round in it is a reason people still say yes when you ask them to come. And one of these years, choose a top that's only for you, take people strong enough to get there and back, and go. They'll all come home, the way they always do with you. This time, I hope you stand on it.
